newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe faces hard talks with donors to win aid.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe faces hard talks with donors to win aid.

text.p: Zimbabwe faces tough talks next week with Western donors in a bid to win financial backing for a five-year economic reform programme it plans to launch later this year, local economic analysts said on Thursday.
"So far, all we have received is support in principle. The small but very important details are still to be discussed," said economic consultant John Robertson.
"Although, we are expecting positive results in the end, I think everyone is also aware the talks could be hard, but for the good," he told Reuters.

World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF) missions from Washington are expected in Zimbabwe next week to open detailed negotiations on the country's financial needs for the Zimbabwe Programme for Economic and Social Transformation (ZIMPREST).
World Bank chief representative in Harare David Cook told Reuters it was inappropriate for him to discuss the issue and the IMF's Robert Franco was unavailable for comment.
But last month Franco told a news conference the talks would focus on the southern African country's perennial battle against high government spending and its budget deficit.

"It would be a pity if they got here and we have not done our homework," he said then, saying Zimbabwe needed to demonstrate that its plan to cut the budget deficit to 8.6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by next June from 10.1 percent in the last financial year was on track.

Many Zimbabwean economic analysts believe the deficit may actually balloon to around 12 percent following government's recent award of 20 percent salary rises to civil servants after a crippling three-week strike.
Some of the civil servants, mostly nurses and doctors, went back on strike this week to press for demands for higher pay increases of up to 60 percent.
Although President Robert Mugabe's government has opened talks with the strikers over their demands, analysts say it cannot afford further increases.

"As it is, everyone is expecting that the talks with the donors will be hard...and the government will be keen to ensure it is sending the right signals," said Savvas Kyriakides, managing director of economic and share market analysts Dataworld.
Zimbabwe Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa also refused on Thursday to discuss the forthcoming talks, although he said last week both the World Bank and the IMF were generally supportive.
"No money has been pledged yet," he said of media reports which quoted him as saying last week the IMF had agreed to fund Zimbabwe's reforms to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars.
The Bank and the Fund cut some financial support to the country in 1995 when the government failed to implement some cost-saving measures.
Many of Zimbabwe's big Western donors say they will wait for its agreement with the World Bank and the IMF before deciding on their own levels of support for the reform programme.
